title: The History of Cabbage — The Vegetable That Fed Civilizations
fullText: The year is 1770. A wooden ship is dying in the middle of the sea. Not from a storm, not from an enemy, from something far quieter. One by one, the sailors are falling. Their gums bleed. Their teeth loosen and drop. Old wounds healed years ago, split open again as if they were fresh. Men who were strong a month ago can barely stand. They are thousands of miles from land. There is no doctor, no cure, no way home in time. For hundreds of years, this was the terror of every long voyage. It killed more sailors than storms and battles combined. Whole crews vanished this way, swallowed by the sea. But this ship is different because down in its dark belly, packed in heavy wooden barrels, sits a secret. a strange sour smelling food that most of the crew didn't even want to eat. And that food is about to keep every single one of them alive. Cabbage. Just cabbage. Now open your refrigerator. It's probably still in there, round, green, cheap, the most forgettable thing on the shelf. You've walked past it a thousand times without a second thought. But that plain vegetable saved those sailors. It fed hungry armies. It survived brutal winters. It crossed oceans. And one day it would even leave the earth. So here's the question this whole story is going to answer. How did one plain green vegetable, the one sitting quietly in your kitchen right now, quietly help feed civilizations? Not kings, not emperors, real people, mothers, farmers, sailors, children. Let's find out. Before cabbage changed human life, travel back with me. Way back, thousands of years, long before cities, long before markets, long before anyone wrote a single word down. Picture the coast of Europe. Cold wind, gray waves crashing against rocky cliffs, salt in the air, and clinging to those rocks growing where almost nothing else could survive. Is a tough little plant. Its leaves are thick, a little bitter, a little tough to chew. Salt spray washes over it every day and still it holds on. This is wild sea cabbage, the great great grandparent of every cabbage in the world. Nobody planted it. Nobody cared for it. It simply grew wild and forgotten on the edge of the land. Now picture the people who lived nearby. Their lives were hard. Every single day was a search for food. Summer was kind. Fruit ripened. Plants grew. There was enough to eat. But then came the enemy that no one could fight. Winter. When the cold arrived, the world seemed to shut down. Plants died. Fields turned brown and empty. The soft green food of summer simply vanished. And here was the terrible problem. How do you keep eating when nothing will grow? Fresh vegetables almost never lasted through the cold months. They rotted. They froze. They turned to mush. Families watched their food disappear and waited, hungry for spring. Winter was not just cold. Winter was dangerous. Winter could kill. Think about how frightening that was. These early people had no stores, no way to buy food from far away. If the land around them stopped giving, there was nowhere else to turn. Their whole lives followed the seasons. When the weather was warm, they gathered as much as they could. When the cold came, they held their breath and hoped what they had saved would be enough. Some years it was, some years it was not. So people searched, they tasted everything. They tried every plant they could find, learning slowly which ones would feed them and which ones would harm them. Some plants made them sick, some kept them alive. It was slow, careful learning, passed from parent to child over many lifetimes. And somewhere along that rocky coast, someone found the tough little plant clinging to the cliffs. They pulled off a leaf. They chewed it. It was bitter, but it filled the belly, and it was there, growing strong, even when the weather turned cruel. That small, stubborn plant was about to change everything. But how does a wild bitter weed on a cliff become food for millions? That answer begins with a few patient farmers. From wild plant to farm crop move now to warmer shores, the sunny coast of the Mediterranean Sea. Blue water, bright light, and people who were no longer just wanderers searching for food. These people had learned something powerful. They had learned to farm. Instead of hunting for wild plants, they began to grow them. And this simple idea would quietly reshape the whole world. Here's how it worked. A farmer would look out over their plants. And every farmer noticed the same thing. Some plants were better than others. Some had bigger leaves. Some grew stronger. Some tasted less bitter. So the farmer made a choice, a small choice. They saved seeds from the best plants, the strongest, the leafiest, the ones that gave the most food. Then they planted those seeds the next year. And they did it again and again and again. Look at what that means. One farmer chooses the best plant. Then their child does the same. Then their grandchild. Season after season, life after life. Slowly something amazing happened. The leaves grew larger. The plants grew fuller. The bitter taste faded away. The tough, wild weed of the cliffs was becoming something new, something softer, something bigger, something dependable. This slow, patient work is called domestication. It's how wild plants become farm crops. And it wasn't done by scientists or kings. It was done by ordinary farmers, one careful choice at a time. The wild sea cabbage was being tamed. And it wasn't just becoming one plant. From that same wild ancestor, farmers would shape many different vegetables over time, but the leafy one, the one wrapped tight into a round head, became the cabbage we know today. Soon, this new reliable plant reached ancient Greece. The Greeks grew it, they ate it, and they trusted it because it was easy to grow, and it rarely let them down. Then the cabbage traveled to a place that would spread it across a huge part of the world, Rome. And in Rome, this humble plant was about to become something much stranger than food. The vegetable they believed in ancient Rome, a world of stone streets, crowded cities, and busy, noisy markets. Meet one of the most powerful men in the whole city. His name is Kato, a senator, a war hero, a man whose words could shake the entire Roman government. And he wants to tell you about his favorite thing in the world, cabbage. Kato wrote a whole book about running a farm. And when he reached the subject of cabbage, he could not stop. He believed this simple vegetable was almost magic. He said it could heal wounds, calm a sick stomach, cure aching heads and tired eyes. If you were ill, Kato had one answer. Eat cabbage. Rub it on the hurt. Trust it. Was he right? Not really. But this is what matters. People believed him. To the Romans, cabbage wasn't just food. It was medicine, protection, a kind of magic you could grow right in your own garden. They even ate it at their wildest parties. Before a long night of wine, Romans would swallow raw cabbage first. They believed it kept them from getting drunk so they could drink more and last longer. And then there's the strangest part of all. Some Romans believed that the urine of a person who ate lots of cabbage became a medicine, too. They would save it, warm it, and use it to treat the sick. Kato swore he had seen it work. It sounds unbelievable today, but stop and think about what it tells us. A tough little plant from a windy cliff had climbed all the way to the top of the greatest empire on earth. Powerful men trusted it with their health. Poor families trusted it with their lives, and they trusted it because it never let them down. It was easy to grow, cheap enough for anyone, reliable season after season. It fed the rich and the poor, the city and the countryside, even the soldiers marching across the empire. Cabbage was no longer just something you ate. It was something you believed in. But belief is easy at a warm Roman feast. The real test was coming. A test that returned every single year. A test that decided who lived and who died. Winter, the vegetable that saved winter. Let's return to the cold. Imagine a small village long ago. The last leaves have fallen. The sky is gray. The wind bites at your skin. Winter has arrived and with it comes the oldest fear of all. The fields are empty. Nothing grows. The fresh food of summer is gone. Picture a family inside a small home. A mother looks at what little food is left. She has children to feed. And she knows something frightening. There will be no fresh food for months. Not for weeks, for months. So ask yourself the question they had to ask. How do you survive six long months with nothing fresh to eat? This was not a small problem. This was the difference between life and death every single year. Most vegetables could not help. They spoiled too fast. They rotted in days. They were beautiful in summer and useless by the time the snow came. But cabbage was different. Cabbage was tough. Cabbage was patient. Cabbage could last. Families learned to store it. And they got clever about how. Some dug deep pits in the ground and buried their cabbages, where the cool earth kept them fresh far longer than the open air ever could. Some kept them in dark, cold cellars beneath their homes, stacked and waiting. Some stored them with the roots still attached, hanging in cool corners, holding on to life a little longer. A single cabbage could last for weeks, sometimes even months. And a family with a store of cabbage had something priceless. They had time. They had a full belly in the dead of winter. They had a fighting chance. Sit with what that meant. Day after day outside, the world was frozen and silent. There was no fresh food anywhere for miles. Other families, without a store of their own, grew thin and weak as the winter dragged on. Some did not make it to spring. But a family with cabbage in the cellar had a little more hope than the rest, a little more strength, a few more meals between them and hunger. So a simple question hung over every home when the cold arrived. How much food did you save? And will it be enough? For families with cabbage, the answer was a little kinder than it might have been. Picture that mother again. It's the coldest, darkest part of the year. Outside, the ground is frozen solid, but she reaches into the cellar and pulls out a cabbage she stored back in the autumn. That cabbage becomes soup, warm and filling, enough to feed her children one more night. That is not a small thing. That is survival. All across the cold parts of the world, families were doing the same. leaning on this stubborn green vegetable to carry them through the hardest season. Cabbage had become a kind of insurance, a promise, a quiet guard standing between families and starvation. But storing a fresh cabbage could only take you so far. Eventually, even the toughest cabbage would spoil. So, humans asked a bigger question. What if you could make food last not for months, but through the whole winter and far, far beyond? The answer would change history. And it started with nothing more than salt, thyme, and a little bit of magic. The secret that crossed the world here was the problem that still remained. Fresh cabbage, no matter how carefully you stored it, would eventually go bad. Nature always won in the end. So, people needed a new idea. Not just a way to store cabbage, a way to change it, a way to make it last far longer than nature ever allowed. And what they discovered feels almost like magic, but it's real and it's beautifully simple. It's called fermentation. Let me show you how it works. It only takes two things you might not expect. Salt and thyme. Here's the secret. You take fresh cabbage and slice it thin. Then you mix it with salt and press it down tight so the leaves sit in their own juices with no air. Then you wait. And while you wait, something wonderful happens. Tiny living things, far too small to see, begin to feed on the cabbage. They are helpful, not harmful. As they work, they slowly change it. They keep the bad rot away. They turn the taste sharp and sour and rich. Days pass, then weeks, and when it's ready, the cabbage has become something new. Sauerkraut. The word simply means sour cabbage. And it was one of the most important food discoveries humans ever made. Because now the food lasted, not for days, not for weeks, for months and months. Long after fresh cabbage would have rotted away. And it didn't just survive. It kept people strong and healthy through the long dark months when no other food was around. Once winter was a season of fear and empty bowls. Now families could fill a barrel with sauerkraut in the autumn and eat well until spring. From the villages of Germany to the frozen countryside of Russia and Eastern Europe, families packed barrels of it deep into their cellars. Sour cabbage became a winter treasure across half a continent. But this is where the story grows far bigger than one family's cellar. Because this secret was about to travel further than anyone could dream. Let me tell you something that surprises almost everyone. Think of sauerkraut, sour cabbage. Most people picture Germany. It even has a German name, but the story may begin on the other side of the world. In China, more than 2,000 years ago. Picture the workers building the Great Wall of China. A wall so vast it climbed over mountains and crossed deserts, taking lifetimes to build. Those workers needed food that would last. cheap food, food that wouldn't spoil in the cold. So, they ate cabbage. And to keep it through the winter, they let it ferment. Sour cabbage feeding the builders of one of the greatest things human hands have ever made. That alone is amazing. But the story doesn't stop there. Roll forward a thousand years and meet one of the most feared men in all of history, Genghask Khan. His armies swept out of the east like a storm, conquering land after land, crossing thousands of miles. And an army that huge needs one thing above everything else. Food that travels. And some say that as the Mongol armies rode west, they carried fermented cabbage with them all the way to the edge of Europe. Now, is every piece of this story certain? No. History gets blurry this far back. The Romans soured their cabbage, too, and they may have passed the idea along as well. But sit with the possibility for a moment. The most German food in the world may have been born at the Great Wall of China and carried across all of Asia on the backs of Mongol war horses. That is the kind of secret hiding inside a simple barrel of sour cabbage. And it shows us something important. Fermentation didn't just save one family through one winter. It gave cabbage a superpower. It could now cross deserts, follow armies, travel further than the very people who first grew it. Cabbage had learned to beat time. And now it was crossing the world. But the Mongols were not the only ones who found this secret. Far away in another land, a different people were solving the very same problem. In a way, all their own. the buried treasure of Korea. Travel now to Korea, a land of green mountains and long cold winters. And a people who turned surviving that cold into something the whole country would come to love. They took the same simple idea the rest of the world was finding. And they made it unmistakably their own. Kimchi. Here's how they did it. They took cabbage and other vegetables. They added salt. They added spice, bold and red and full of fire. And then they let it ferment, just like the sour cabbage of the West, but with a flavor all its own. But the Koreans added something clever, something you might not expect. They buried it. They packed the kimchi into large clay pots and they placed those pots deep in the ground. Why? Because underground, the temperature stays steady, not too warm, not too cold. The earth itself became a giant natural refrigerator, holding the kimchi at just the right coolness to last the whole winter through. Buried treasure, not gold, not jewels, food, and making it was not a quiet, lonely job. Picture a whole village coming together as the cold drew near. families, neighbors, grandmothers, and children all working side by side, chopping, salting, mixing, filling pot after pot after pot. It became a season all its own. A time of year when the whole community joined hands to prepare for the months ahead together. Enough kimchi for every family, enough to last until the world turned green again. And over the long years, kimchi became far more than food. It became part of who the Korean people were. A taste of home, a flavor passed from mother to daughter, grandmother to grandchild for hundreds and hundreds of years. Still today, it appears at nearly every meal in nearly every home. And this is the beautiful thing. On one side of the world, people salted cabbage into sauerkraut. On the other side, people buried it as kimchi. They had never met. They spoke different languages. They lived worlds apart. But they all asked the very same question. How do we make our food last? And so many of them found the very same answer hiding in the leaves of one common cabbage. The same problem solved again and again all around the world. But there was still one place cabbage had not yet conquered. A place with no soil, no gardens, no ground at all. The open sea. the vegetable that conquered the ocean. Some of the hardest journeys in all of history happened at sea. Imagine climbing aboard a sailing ship hundreds of years ago. You're leaving land behind for months, maybe longer. Ahead of you is nothing but endless water. There are no farms out here, no markets, no gardens, just the ship, the crew, and the waves. And this created a deadly problem. Fresh food ran out fast. And when it did, sailors began to fall sick with something terrible. It was called scurvy. Scurvy was a sailor's nightmare. Without fresh food, the bodies slowly broke down. Men grew weak. Their gums bled. Their old wounds opened again. Their teeth fell out and far too many of them died thousands of miles from home. This was a real terror of the sea. On some voyages, more sailors died from scurvy than from storms, shipwrecks, or battles. A ship might set out full of strong, healthy men and limp home with only a handful still standing. For a long time, no one understood why. Captains tried everything. Nothing seemed to work. The mystery held on, and the dying continued. But the answer, it turned out, was hiding in a barrel. Meet a famous sea captain named James Cook. Cook sailed on some of the longest voyages of his time into distant parts of the world. And he was determined to keep his crew alive. He was determined to beat Scurvy. So he loaded his ships with a special cargo. Barrel after barrel of sauerkraut. That same sour fermented cabbage. The food that had saved families through winter was now going to sea. But Cook had a problem. His sailors took one look at the strange, sour, foreign cabbage and refused to touch it. So, Cook did something clever, something a little sneaky. He stopped offering it to the crew at all. Instead, he served the sauerkraut only at the officer's table. The captain and his officers ate it happily, right where the sailors could see, and human nature did the rest. Soon, the crew wanted it. If it was good enough for the officers, they thought, surely it was good enough for them. They began asking for the very cabbage Cook had kept from them. It worked perfectly. On voyages longer than any sailors had ever survived before, Cook lost not a single man to scurvy. Not one. Now, think about what that truly means. For all of history, the ocean had a wall around it. Sail too far, stay out too long, and your crew would sicken and die. The sea kept people close to the shore, but a barrel of sour cabbage helped break that wall. Because sailors could finally survive the journey, this single vegetable helped human beings cross entire oceans, reach lands they had never seen, map the whole face of the planet. Kings are remembered for conquering countries, but a plain green vegetable helped humanity conquer the sea. The vegetable that left the earth. Now, let's leap forward into the modern world. For most of our story, cabbage came from small gardens and family farms. Then, everything sped up. Farms grew huge. Trucks and trains and cold storage carried cabbage fresh across whole countries. It filled the bright shelves of the supermarket, cheap and ready all year round. But here's the twist most people miss. Refrigeration didn't save cabbage. Cabbage never needed saving. Long before freezers and cold trucks, this vegetable had already beaten winter. Already beaten spoiling, already crossed deserts and oceans. It had been solving those problems for thousands of years. So, the modern world didn't rescue cabbage. The modern world just gave it new places to go. Picture the millions of people who left their homelands for good. families boarding ships, crossing oceans to start over in strange new countries. They couldn't carry much, but so many of them carried this. A few cabbage seeds and the old family way of making sauerkraut or kimchi. A taste of home tucked into a brand new life. And so cabbage spread again, not with armies this time, with ordinary people chasing a better future. It put down roots on every continent on Earth. Wherever humans went, the cabbage went too. It even got tangled up in the biggest storms of history. About a 100red years ago, during World War I, feeling against Germany ran so hot in America that sauerkraut, sour cabbage, suddenly sounded like the enemy. So, people refused to even say the word. They gave it a new one. Liberty cabbage. Think about that. A simple vegetable pulled right into the middle of a world war. A food important enough that people argued over its very name. By now you might think cabbage had been everywhere, every kitchen, every country, every continent. But it had one frontier left, one place no cabbage had ever gone up. In 2008, a young scientist named Yi So Yan became the first Korean ever to fly into space all the way to the space station high above our heads. And she wanted to bring Kimchi. But there was a serious problem. Kimchi is alive. It's full of tiny living things still slowly fermenting away. And out in space, sealed inside a pouch, those living things could keep working, building up gas, even bursting the package. On a spacecraft packed with delicate equipment that is dangerous, so an entire team of Korean scientists went to work. For years, they studied and tested and reinvented this ancient food. They found a way to calm the living bacteria and make the kimchi safe without losing the taste of home. and they did it. So when that rocket tore off the earth and climbed into the black of space, cabbage went with it. Stop and picture the whole journey for just a second. A tough, bitter weed clinging to a cold and rocky cliff. The same plant thousands of years later, floating high above the planet, carried into space by people who could not imagine leaving the Earth without it. From the edge of the sea to the edge of space. That is how far one humble vegetable has traveled. Which brings us all the way back down back home to your kitchen. Your kitchen. Come home now. Back to a modern kitchen. Warm and familiar. The soft hum of the refrigerator. A hand reaches out and opens the door. Cold air drifts out. And there it is. A cabbage. Round green. Heavy. It looks exactly the same as it did at the very start of our story. Plain, simple, easy to overlook. But you see it differently now, don't you? Hold it for a moment and think about everything folded inside those leaves. A wild plant on a windy cliff. The Roman senator who swore it was medicine. The dark cellar that carried a family through the frozen months. The sour cabbage that may have ridden west with Genghaskhan. The clay pots of kimchi buried in the Korean earth by whole villages working side by side. The barrels of sauerkraut that kept sailors alive long enough to map the world. And a pouch of that same ancient food floating in space high above the planet. All of it. Every story folded into that one ordinary cabbage on your shelf. And this is the strangest part of all. You walked right past it. We all do every single day without a second glance. Because it's cheap. Because it's always there. Because it never asks us for anything. We forgot it was ever a hero. But it never forgot us. The vegetable that fed kings. So here we are. A person standing in a kitchen holding an ordinary cabbage. It doesn't look like a hero. It never did. But you know the truth now. It survived the winters that starved whole villages. It fed the poor when they had nothing else. It crossed deserts with armies and oceans with explorers. It became sauerkraut and kimchi and 100 dishes with 100 names. It helped humans map the whole planet. And then it followed us off it. It quietly held up civilizations while history remembered kings. It never wore a crown. It never led an army. It never ruled an empire. It never even needed us. We needed it. So the next time you open your refrigerator and see that plain green cabbage sitting on the shelf, you won't just see a vegetable. You'll see one of the quiet heroes that carried us all the way
fullTextVi: Năm đó là 1770. Một con tàu gỗ đang chết dần giữa biển. Không phải từ một cơn bão, không phải từ kẻ thù, từ một thứ gì đó yên tĩnh hơn rất nhiều. Từng người một, các thủy thủ đang rơi xuống. Nướu của họ chảy máu. Răng của họ lung lay và rụng xuống. Những vết thương cũ đã lành từ nhiều năm trước, lại nứt ra như còn mới. Những người đàn ông mạnh mẽ một tháng trước gần như không thể đứng vững. Họ cách đất liền hàng ngàn dặm. Không có bác sĩ, không có thuốc chữa, không có đường về nhà kịp thời. Trong hàng trăm năm, đây là nỗi kinh hoàng của mỗi chuyến đi dài. Nó giết chết nhiều thủy thủ hơn cả bão và trận chiến cộng lại. Toàn bộ thủy thủ đoàn biến mất theo cách này, bị biển nuốt chửng. Nhưng con tàu này thì khác vì bên dưới phần bụng tối tăm của nó, được đóng gói trong những chiếc thùng gỗ nặng nề, ẩn chứa một bí mật. một món ăn có mùi chua lạ mà hầu hết cả đoàn thậm chí không muốn ăn. Và thức ăn đó sắp giữ cho mỗi người trong số họ sống sót. Bắp cải. Bắp cải thôi. Bây giờ hãy mở tủ lạnh của bạn. Có lẽ nó vẫn còn ở đó, tròn, xanh, rẻ tiền, thứ đáng quên nhất trên kệ. Bạn đã đi ngang qua nó hàng nghìn lần mà không hề suy nghĩ. Nhưng loại rau đơn giản đó đã cứu được những thủy thủ đó. Nó nuôi sống những đội quân đói khát. Nó sống sót qua mùa đông khắc nghiệt. Nó vượt qua đại dương. Và một ngày nào đó nó thậm chí sẽ rời khỏi trái đất. Vậy đây là câu hỏi mà toàn bộ câu chuyện này sẽ trả lời. Làm thế nào mà một loại rau xanh đơn giản, thứ đang ngồi lặng lẽ trong căn bếp của bạn lúc này, lại lặng lẽ giúp nuôi sống các nền văn minh? Không phải vua, không phải hoàng đế, không phải người thật, mẹ, nông dân, thủy thủ, trẻ em. Hãy cùng tìm hiểu. Trước khi bắp cải thay đổi cuộc đời con người, hãy cùng tôi quay trở lại. Quay ngược lại, hàng ngàn năm, rất lâu trước các thành phố, rất lâu trước các thị trường, rất lâu trước khi có người viết ra một từ nào. Hình ảnh bờ biển châu Âu. Gió lạnh, những con sóng xám xịt xô vào vách đá, muối trong không khí và bám vào những tảng đá ngày càng phát triển mà hầu như không thứ gì khác có thể tồn tại được. Là một loại cây nhỏ cứng rắn. Lá của nó dày, hơi đắng, hơi dai khi nhai. Xịt muối hàng ngày lên nó mà nó vẫn bám. Đây là bắp cải biển hoang dã, ông cố của mọi loại bắp cải trên thế giới. Không ai trồng nó. Không ai quan tâm đến nó. Nó chỉ đơn giản là mọc hoang và bị lãng quên ở rìa đất. Bây giờ hãy hình dung những người sống gần đó. Cuộc sống của họ thật khó khăn. Mỗi ngày đều là một cuộc tìm kiếm thức ăn. Mùa hè thật tử tế. Quả đã chín. Cây cối đã lớn lên. Có đủ để ăn. Nhưng rồi kẻ thù xuất hiện mà không ai có thể chống lại được. Mùa đông. Khi cái lạnh ập đến, thế giới dường như đóng cửa. Cây cối chết. Những cánh đồng chuyển sang màu nâu và trống trải. Thức ăn xanh mềm của mùa hè đơn giản biến mất. Và đây là vấn đề khủng khiếp. Làm thế nào để bạn tiếp tục ăn khi không có gì sẽ phát triển? Rau tươi hầu như không bao giờ tồn tại được qua những tháng lạnh giá. Chúng đã thối rữa. Họ đóng băng. Họ biến thành bột nhão. segments.text: The year is 1770.
segments.viText: Năm đó là 1770.

segments.text: A wooden ship is dying in the middle of the sea.
segments.viText: Một con tàu gỗ đang chết dần giữa biển.

segments.text: Not from a storm, not from an enemy, from something far quieter.
segments.viText: Không phải từ một cơn bão, không phải từ kẻ thù, từ một thứ gì đó yên tĩnh hơn rất nhiều.

segments.text: One by one, the sailors are falling.
segments.viText: Từng người một, các thủy thủ đang rơi xuống.

segments.text: Their gums bleed.
segments.viText: Nướu của họ chảy máu.

segments.text: Their teeth loosen and drop.
segments.viText: Răng của họ lung lay và rụng xuống.

segments.text: Old wounds healed years ago, split open again as if they were fresh.
segments.viText: Những vết thương cũ đã lành từ nhiều năm trước, lại nứt ra như còn mới.

segments.text: Men who were strong a month ago can barely stand.
segments.viText: Những người đàn ông mạnh mẽ một tháng trước gần như không thể đứng vững.

segments.text: They are thousands of miles from land.
segments.viText: Họ cách đất liền hàng ngàn dặm.

segments.text: There is no doctor, no cure, no way home in time.
segments.viText: Không có bác sĩ, không có thuốc chữa, không có đường về nhà kịp thời.

segments.text: For hundreds of years, this was the terror of every long voyage.
segments.viText: Trong hàng trăm năm, đây là nỗi kinh hoàng của mỗi chuyến đi dài.

segments.text: It killed more sailors than storms and battles combined.
segments.viText: Nó giết chết nhiều thủy thủ hơn cả bão và trận chiến cộng lại.

segments.text: Whole crews vanished this way, swallowed by the sea.
segments.viText: Toàn bộ thủy thủ đoàn biến mất theo cách này, bị biển nuốt chửng.

segments.text: But this ship is different because down in its dark belly, packed in heavy wooden barrels, sits a secret.
segments.viText: Nhưng con tàu này thì khác vì bên dưới phần bụng tối tăm của nó, được đóng gói trong những chiếc thùng gỗ nặng nề, ẩn chứa một bí mật.

segments.text: a strange sour smelling food that most of the crew didn't even want to eat.
segments.viText: một món ăn có mùi chua lạ mà hầu hết cả đoàn thậm chí không muốn ăn.

segments.text: And that food is about to keep every single one of them alive.
segments.viText: Và thức ăn đó sắp giữ cho mỗi người trong số họ sống sót.

segments.text: Cabbage.
segments.viText: Bắp cải.

segments.text: Just cabbage.
segments.viText: Bắp cải thôi.

segments.text: Now open your refrigerator.
segments.viText: Bây giờ hãy mở tủ lạnh của bạn.

segments.text: It's probably still in there, round, green, cheap, the most forgettable thing on the shelf.
segments.viText: Có lẽ nó vẫn còn ở đó, tròn, xanh, rẻ tiền, thứ đáng quên nhất trên kệ.

segments.text: You've walked past it a thousand times without a second thought.
segments.viText: Bạn đã đi ngang qua nó hàng nghìn lần mà không hề suy nghĩ.

segments.text: But that plain vegetable saved those sailors.
segments.viText: Nhưng loại rau đơn giản đó đã cứu được những thủy thủ đó.

segments.text: It fed hungry armies.
segments.viText: Nó nuôi sống những đội quân đói khát.

segments.text: It survived brutal winters.
segments.viText: Nó sống sót qua mùa đông khắc nghiệt.

segments.text: It crossed oceans.
segments.viText: Nó vượt qua đại dương.

segments.text: And one day it would even leave the earth.
segments.viText: Và một ngày nào đó nó thậm chí sẽ rời khỏi trái đất.

segments.text: So here's the question this whole story is going to answer.
segments.viText: Vậy đây là câu hỏi mà toàn bộ câu chuyện này sẽ trả lời.

segments.text: How did one plain green vegetable, the one sitting quietly in your kitchen right now, quietly help feed civilizations?
segments.viText: Làm thế nào mà một loại rau xanh đơn giản, thứ đang ngồi lặng lẽ trong căn bếp của bạn lúc này, lại lặng lẽ giúp nuôi sống các nền văn minh?

segments.text: Not kings, not emperors, real people, mothers, farmers, sailors, children.
segments.viText: Không phải vua, không phải hoàng đế, không phải người thật, mẹ, nông dân, thủy thủ, trẻ em.

segments.text: Let's find out.
segments.viText: Hãy cùng tìm hiểu.

segments.text: Before cabbage changed human life, travel back with me.
segments.viText: Trước khi bắp cải thay đổi cuộc đời con người, hãy cùng tôi quay trở lại.

segments.text: Way back, thousands of years, long before cities, long before markets, long before anyone wrote a single word down.
segments.viText: Quay ngược lại, hàng ngàn năm, rất lâu trước các thành phố, rất lâu trước các thị trường, rất lâu trước khi có người viết ra một từ nào.

segments.text: Picture the coast of Europe.
segments.viText: Hình ảnh bờ biển châu Âu.

segments.text: Cold wind, gray waves crashing against rocky cliffs, salt in the air, and clinging to those rocks growing where almost nothing else could survive.
segments.viText: Gió lạnh, những con sóng xám xịt xô vào vách đá, muối trong không khí và bám vào những tảng đá ngày càng phát triển mà hầu như không thứ gì khác có thể tồn tại được.

segments.text: Is a tough little plant.
segments.viText: Là một loại cây nhỏ cứng rắn.

segments.text: Its leaves are thick, a little bitter, a little tough to chew.
segments.viText: Lá của nó dày, hơi đắng, hơi dai khi nhai.

segments.text: Salt spray washes over it every day and still it holds on.
segments.viText: Xịt muối hàng ngày lên nó mà nó vẫn bám.

segments.text: This is wild sea cabbage, the great great grandparent of every cabbage in the world.
segments.viText: Đây là bắp cải biển hoang dã, ông cố của mọi loại bắp cải trên thế giới.

segments.text: Nobody planted it.
segments.viText: Không ai trồng nó.

segments.text: Nobody cared for it.
segments.viText: Không ai quan tâm đến nó.

segments.text: It simply grew wild and forgotten on the edge of the land.
segments.viText: Nó chỉ đơn giản là mọc hoang và bị lãng quên ở rìa đất.

segments.text: Now picture the people who lived nearby.
segments.viText: Bây giờ hãy hình dung những người sống gần đó.

segments.text: Their lives were hard.
segments.viText: Cuộc sống của họ thật khó khăn.

segments.text: Every single day was a search for food.
segments.viText: Mỗi ngày đều là một cuộc tìm kiếm thức ăn.

segments.text: Summer was kind.
segments.viText: Mùa hè thật tử tế.

segments.text: Fruit ripened.
segments.viText: Quả đã chín.

segments.text: Plants grew.
segments.viText: Cây cối đã lớn lên.

segments.text: There was enough to eat.
segments.viText: Có đủ để ăn.

segments.text: But then came the enemy that no one could fight.
segments.viText: Nhưng rồi kẻ thù xuất hiện mà không ai có thể chống lại được.

segments.text: Winter.
segments.viText: Mùa đông.

segments.text: When the cold arrived, the world seemed to shut down.
segments.viText: Khi cái lạnh ập đến, thế giới dường như đóng cửa.

segments.text: Plants died.
segments.viText: Cây cối chết.

segments.text: Fields turned brown and empty.
segments.viText: Những cánh đồng chuyển sang màu nâu và trống trải.

segments.text: The soft green food of summer simply vanished.
segments.viText: Thức ăn xanh mềm của mùa hè đơn giản biến mất.

segments.text: And here was the terrible problem.
segments.viText: Và đây là vấn đề khủng khiếp.

segments.text: How do you keep eating when nothing will grow?
segments.viText: Làm thế nào để bạn tiếp tục ăn khi không có gì sẽ phát triển?

segments.text: Fresh vegetables almost never lasted through the cold months.
segments.viText: Rau tươi hầu như không bao giờ tồn tại được qua những tháng lạnh giá.

segments.text: They rotted.
segments.viText: Chúng đã thối rữa.

segments.text: They froze.
segments.viText: Họ đóng băng.

segments.text: They turned to mush.
segments.viText: Họ biến thành bột nhão.

segments.text: Families watched their food disappear and waited, hungry for spring.
segments.viText: Các gia đình nhìn thức ăn biến mất và chờ đợi, khao khát mùa xuân.

segments.text: Winter was not just cold.
segments.viText: Mùa đông không chỉ lạnh.

segments.text: Winter was dangerous.
segments.viText: Mùa đông thật nguy hiểm.

segments.viText: Hãy nghĩ xem điều đó đáng sợ đến mức nào.

segments.text: These early people had no stores, no way to buy food from far away.
segments.viText: Những người đầu tiên này không có cửa hàng, không có cách nào để mua thực phẩm từ xa.

segments.text: If the land around them stopped giving, there was nowhere else to turn.
segments.viText: Nếu đất xung quanh họ ngừng trao đổi, sẽ không còn nơi nào khác để quay đầu.

segments.text: Their whole lives followed the seasons.
segments.viText: Toàn bộ cuộc sống của họ theo các mùa.

segments.text: When the weather was warm, they gathered as much as they could.
segments.viText: Khi thời tiết ấm áp, họ tụ tập càng nhiều càng tốt.

segments.text: When the cold came, they held their breath and hoped what they had saved would be enough.
segments.viText: Khi cái lạnh ập đến, họ nín thở và hy vọng những gì mình dành dụm được là đủ.

segments.text: Some years it was, some years it was not.
segments.viText: Có năm thì có, có năm thì không.

segments.text: So people searched, they tasted everything.
segments.viText: Vì thế mọi người tìm kiếm, họ nếm thử mọi thứ.

segments.text: They tried every plant they could find, learning slowly which ones would feed them and which ones would harm them.
segments.viText: Họ thử mọi loại cây có thể tìm được, từ từ tìm hiểu xem cây nào sẽ cho chúng ăn và cây nào sẽ gây hại cho chúng.

segments.text: Some plants made them sick, some kept them alive.
segments.viText: Một số cây làm chúng bị bệnh, một số giữ chúng sống.

segments.text: It was slow, careful learning, passed from parent to child over many lifetimes.
segments.viText: Đó là sự học hỏi chậm rãi, cẩn thận, được truyền từ cha mẹ sang con cái trong nhiều kiếp.

segments.text: And somewhere along that rocky coast, someone found the tough little plant clinging to the cliffs.
segments.viText: Và ở đâu đó dọc theo bờ biển đầy đá đó, ai đó đã tìm thấy một loài thực vật nhỏ bé cứng rắn đang bám vào vách đá.

segments.text: They pulled off a leaf.
segments.viText: Họ nhổ một chiếc lá.

segments.text: They chewed it.
segments.viText: Họ nhai nó.

segments.text: It was bitter, but it filled the belly, and it was there, growing strong, even when the weather turned cruel.
segments.viText: Nó đắng nghét, nhưng nó lấp đầy bụng, và nó vẫn ở đó, ngày càng mạnh mẽ, ngay cả khi thời tiết trở nên khắc nghiệt.

segments.text: That small, stubborn plant was about to change everything.
segments.viText: Cái cây nhỏ bé bướng bỉnh đó sắp sửa thay đổi mọi thứ.

segments.text: But how does a wild bitter weed on a cliff become food for millions?
segments.viText: Nhưng làm thế nào mà một loại cỏ đắng hoang trên vách đá lại có thể trở thành thức ăn cho hàng triệu người?

segments.text: That answer begins with a few patient farmers.
segments.viText: Câu trả lời đó bắt đầu từ một số nông dân kiên nhẫn.

segments.text: From wild plant to farm crop move now to warmer shores, the sunny coast of the Mediterranean Sea.
segments.viText: Từ thực vật hoang dã đến cây trồng nông nghiệp, giờ đây hãy chuyển đến những bờ biển ấm áp hơn, bờ biển đầy nắng của Biển Địa Trung Hải.

segments.text: Blue water, bright light, and people who were no longer just wanderers searching for food.
segments.viText: Làn nước trong xanh, ánh sáng rực rỡ và những con người không còn chỉ là những kẻ lang thang tìm kiếm thức ăn.

segments.text: These people had learned something powerful.
segments.viText: Những người này đã học được điều gì đó mạnh mẽ.

segments.text: They had learned to farm.
segments.viText: Họ đã học cách làm trang trại.

segments.text: Instead of hunting for wild plants, they began to grow them.
segments.viText: Thay vì săn lùng thực vật hoang dã, họ bắt đầu trồng chúng.

segments.text: And this simple idea would quietly reshape the whole world.
segments.viText: Và ý tưởng đơn giản này sẽ lặng lẽ định hình lại cả thế giới.

segments.text: Here's how it worked.
segments.viText: Đây là cách nó hoạt động.

segments.text: A farmer would look out over their plants.
segments.viText: Một người nông dân sẽ nhìn ra cây trồng của họ.

segments.text: And every farmer noticed the same thing.
segments.viText: Và mọi nông dân đều nhận thấy điều tương tự.

segments.text: Some plants were better than others.
segments.viText: Một số cây tốt hơn những cây khác.

segments.text: Some had bigger leaves.
segments.viText: Một số có lá lớn hơn.

segments.text: Some grew stronger.
segments.viText: Một số trở nên mạnh mẽ hơn.

segments.text: Some tasted less bitter.
segments.viText: Một số có vị ít đắng hơn.

segments.text: So the farmer made a choice, a small choice.
segments.viText: Thế là người nông dân đã đưa ra một lựa chọn, một lựa chọn nhỏ.

segments.text: They saved seeds from the best plants, the strongest, the leafiest, the ones that gave the most food.
segments.viText: Họ để dành hạt giống từ những cây tốt nhất, khỏe nhất, nhiều lá nhất, những cây cho nhiều thức ăn nhất.

segments.text: Then they planted those seeds the next year.
segments.viText: Sau đó, họ gieo những hạt giống đó vào năm sau.

segments.text: And they did it again and again and again.
segments.viText: Và họ đã làm điều đó nhiều lần.

segments.text: Look at what that means.
segments.viText: Hãy nhìn xem điều đó có nghĩa là gì.

segments.text: One farmer chooses the best plant.
segments.viText: Một nông dân chọn cây tốt nhất.

segments.text: Then their child does the same.
segments.viText: Sau đó con của họ cũng làm như vậy.

segments.text: Then their grandchild.
segments.viText: Sau đó là cháu của họ.

segments.text: Season after season, life after life.
segments.viText: Mùa nối mùa, đời nối tiếp đời.

segments.text: Slowly something amazing happened.
segments.viText: Dần dần một điều gì đó đáng kinh ngạc đã xảy ra.

segments.text: The leaves grew larger.
segments.viText: Những chiếc lá ngày càng lớn hơn.

segments.text: The plants grew fuller.
segments.viText: Cây cối mọc đầy đặn hơn.

segments.text: The bitter taste faded away.
segments.viText: Vị đắng đã nhạt dần.

segments.text: The tough, wild weed of the cliffs was becoming something new, something softer, something bigger, something dependable.
segments.viText: Đám cỏ dại, cứng cỏi trên vách đá đang trở thành một thứ gì đó mới mẻ, một thứ gì đó mềm mại hơn, một thứ gì đó to lớn hơn, một thứ gì đó đáng tin cậy.

segments.text: This slow, patient work is called domestication.
segments.viText: Công việc chậm rãi và kiên nhẫn này được gọi là thuần hóa.

segments.text: It's how wild plants become farm crops.
segments.viText: Đó là cách thực vật hoang dã trở thành cây trồng nông nghiệp.

segments.text: And it wasn't done by scientists or kings.
segments.viText: Và nó không được thực hiện bởi các nhà khoa học hay các vị vua.

segments.text: It was done by ordinary farmers, one careful choice at a time.
segments.viText: Nó được thực hiện bởi những người nông dân bình thường, mỗi lần một sự lựa chọn cẩn thận.

segments.text: The wild sea cabbage was being tamed.

segments.viText: Bạn sẽ thấy một trong những người hùng thầm lặng đã đưa chúng ta đi hết chặng đường
